turn_text: What are the odds that the Farm Bill is going to be rolled into a larger budget package?

I don't think anyone can really predict that right now. I sure can. But what I do think is that it's important for us to move on this and move fast because we want ag senators and House members to be able to determine ag policy and not to have detailed of agriculture policy suddenly being decided at midnight in a closed-door room where there's no one from farm country. And so even if it somehow got rolled in or if the savings from it got included in some kind of package in January, that's fine. But we want to be able to make sure that the policy agreements and the compromise are determined by people on the Agriculture Committee that have worked on this for so long.

Of course, there's compromise needed in many areas on this bill. You mentioned that agriculture wasn't too far apart on the farm section of it. Do you believe there's compromise that can be made in other areas of the farm bill?

I sure. You know, the dairy program that Colin had worked on so hard, Colin Peterson is in the Senate bill, but not the House bill. And so that's clearly an area where given his work on that, where we could work something out. Conservation programs is very close in the numbers. I think that's a positive and should be fairly easy to work out. We've got that transition as we discussed from the Ag subsidies to the crop insurance, and I think that's going to be an area of big compromise, and then taking care of some of these regional issues that we may have with the South. I think people who've been involved in this for a while know that those are always issues but we always seem to be able to resolve them. So I think those are areas of major compromise.

Now, one area that neither one of us have broached as of yet, it appears, is this food nutrition area that is so far apart, 39.5 billion cut on the house side, 4.5 billion cut on the Senate side. Where do you think that will wind up?

Well, I think first of all, let's look at what the Senate did here with strong bipartisan support. a number of Republican senators voted for the Senate version of about $4 billion in cuts on nutrition, food stamps. And those cuts came from closing a loophole, that's how I think of it, in a program of something that needed to be tightened up. There were 18 states that were using a program in a way that most of us believe it was not intended for in terms of leveraging matching funds on heating assistance.

so that was closed up, and that's how we got to that over 4 trillion in cuts. There may be more things we can do with that. Clearly, we'll look at some of the things raised by the House, but this idea that we would have 10 times the number of cuts at a time when a lot of people are still struggling. When the president said that he will veto a bill that has the 40 billion in cuts, we know that the number should be in some territory a closer to the Senate number to be able to get the kind of urban support we are going to need to actually get this bill done. And as for the details, I think that's going to determine by people of good faith as we look at this and see what are things that we can do. But I think we still have to remember that the cuts that the House put in, which were double what the House Act Committee had originally proposed at $20 billion and got up to nearly $40 billion and makes it hard. But I still think there's hope that people want to get this done.
